Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend on their way to the airport calls, thinking they left their passport at home, and asks if you can check and bring it to them right away.
Situation2: They prepare a sermon for Sunday service to guide the congregation in moral decisions.
Story: I was sitting at my desk, surrounded by open books and scattered notes, trying to finish my sermon for Sunday. The topic was about making wise choices and being there for others, and I wanted every word to count. My phone buzzed, and I saw it was Mark, my oldest friend. His voice was frantic—he was halfway to the airport and thought he’d left his passport at home. He begged me to check and, if it was there, to bring it to him immediately. I glanced at the clock. If I left now, I’d lose the quiet hours I’d set aside to finish my sermon, the one my congregation was counting on to help them navigate their own moral crossroads. Mark needed me, but so did my church. I felt the weight of both expectations pressing in, my loyalty as a friend clashing with my responsibility as a pastor. My heart pounded as I stared at my unfinished sermon, Mark’s desperate voice echoing in my mind, torn between two promises I didn’t want to break.
